WIC · An illustrated investigationResources

Available ≠ Accessible / WIC

Getting help buying food shouldn’t be this much work.

WIC—the Special Supplemental Nutrition Program for Women, Infants, and Children—helps eligible pregnant people, new parents, and young children get nutritious food.

It pays for specific groceries and provides nutrition advice, breastfeeding support, and referrals to care.

Providing a benefit isn’t enough. Making it practical to get and keep using is part of the job.

Follow one illustrative parent. Real program rules and research.
All parent and staff dialogue is scripted, not interview testimony.

Start during pregnancy ↓

Next scene ↓
23.3% · Who didn’t know?
Current adult participants asked why they had not enrolled during earlier pregnancies. Data collected in 2019. Population and methodology ↗
22.6% · Who thought they didn’t qualify?
A separate reason reported by the same surveyed subgroup. Do not add these percentages together. USDA findings ↗
What information do I need?
California asks for proof of identity, residence, and income or participation in a qualifying program. Examples can include identification, mail showing your address, and income records or Medi-Cal information. Ask the agency what is acceptable in your situation; one particular document is not the only route. Requirements and examples ↗
Resources & context
2019 survey; current adult participants explaining nonenrollment during prior pregnancies. Separate reasons, not rejection rates or shares of all eligible families. USDA survey, Exhibit 4 ↗ California enrollment ↗

10 / Research pause · benefit use

Some issued benefits go unused.

One example certification period
70% threshold

“High redemption” means using at least 70% of an issued food category.

Share of certification periods reaching that threshold
Southern California · November 2019–June 2023

Mom

Does everyone use everything they receive?

Research context

This study measured how much of each food category people used during a certification period.

Research context

69.6% of periods with produce benefits reached at least 70% use. That does not mean 69.6% of all produce dollars were used.

Mom

So getting the benefit and using it are different things.

Next scene ↓
Continued participation: an association
Discontinuation was 61.7% among periods with under 10% overall redemption versus 13.1% among periods with at least 70%. This is observational, not proof that redemption prevents departure. Continued eligibility was not established.
Resources & context
188,368 participants, with repeat certification periods. Category denominators differ: formula 140,789; produce 365,738; eggs 364,908; whole milk 176,981. Study and tables ↗

Resources & context
California certification varies by category and age at enrollment. Infants certified before six months can be certified through the first birthday month; child certification is generally one year. Mid-certification assessments occur in the specified fifth-to-seventh-month window. Pregnancy and postpartum are distinct certifications. Certification periods ↗ Mid-certification policy ↗

Research context

WIC reached 56.1% of all eligible people in an average month in 2023.

It reached 82.3% of eligible infants, but only 26.9% of eligible four-year-olds.

Research context

These are different age groups. The chart does not measure this family leaving WIC.

Next scene ↓
Already connected to other help
In a separate survey-based analysis, 41.8% of WIC-eligible children ages 1–4 receiving both Medicaid and SNAP were not receiving WIC. This suggests an opportunity for referrals; it is not additive with the national gap. USDA Table 5.1 ↗
Resources & context
2023 modeled eligibility and administrative participation estimates. National gap: 11,829,215 − 6,631,309 = 5,197,906. USDA national and age estimates ↗
